visual.heading: Why this matters
visual.label: The big picture
items: A **variable** is a name that refers to a value.
Store the price once, as `tea_price`, and use the name everywhere.
Change the value in one place, and every calculation follows.
A basket, a game score, a bank balance: each one is a named value.

segments.say: The fix is a variable. A variable is a name that refers to a value.
Asha stores the tea price once, under the name tea price, and uses that name everywhere.
Change the value in one place, and every calculation follows.
Every app you use works like this. Your basket, your game score, your bank balance. Each one is a value with a name.

scenes.title: The idea: values, types and names
scenes.direction: Teach types with the table, then assignment with the diagram, then the label analogy. Then a quiz on types, then a breather.

segments.say: First, values. A value is one piece of data, like 3, or 3.5, or the word tea. And every value has a type.
An int is a whole number. Use it for counts, like two cups.
A float has a decimal point. Use it for prices, like 3.5.
A string is text, and it always sits inside quotation marks. Even a digit becomes text when it is in quotation marks.
And a bool is a yes or no fact: True or False. Is Asha a member? True.

visual.heading: Assignment: name = value
visual.label: The idea
body: Read `=` as **now refers to**, not as "is equal to".
visual.pre:
name         value
 tea_price  =    3
     ^           |
     +-----------+
  Python works out the right side first,
  then connects the name on the left to it.

segments.say: Now, names. Assignment connects a name to a value. The name goes on the left, then the equals sign, then the value.
Python works out the right side first. Then it connects the name on the left to that value.
So read the equals sign as: now refers to. Tea price now refers to 3.

visual.heading: A variable is like a name label
visual.label: Analogy
items: You stick a label on a value. You can move it to a new value at any time.
Where it stops working: two labels can point to the same value.
Moving one label does not move the other.

segments.say: Think of a variable as a name label. You stick it on a value, and you can move it to a new value whenever you like.
The comparison stops working at one point. Two labels can point to the same value.
And moving one label does not move the other.

visual.question: What is the type of the value `"3"`, with quotation marks?
visual.explain: Quotation marks make text. `"3"` is a `str`, not a number.

segments.say: Quick check. Here is the digit 3, inside quotation marks. What is its type?

after.say: C. A string. The quotation marks make it text. Keep this one in mind. It causes a sneaky bug later.

items: Every value has a type.
A variable is a name for a value.
Python works out the right side of `=` first.

scenes.title: Step 1: First variables
scenes.direction: The file types itself in. Teach the rule about quotation marks, then ask the prediction, then reveal. Then the naming rules.

segments.say: Step 1. Asha creates two variables. Customer refers to the text Asha. Tea price refers to the number 3.
Line 4 prints customer. Look closely: there are no quotation marks around it.
Without quotation marks, Python treats a word as a name, and prints the value it refers to. And in Python, a star means times.

after.say: Line 4 prints Asha, the value, not the word customer.
And line 6 multiplies the tea price by 2, so two teas cost 6.

visual.heading: Good names: four rules
visual.label: Naming rules
items: Style (PEP 8): lowercase words joined by underscores, `tea_price`, not `TeaPrice` or `tp`.
Letters, digits and underscores, but **never a digit first**.
Capitals matter: `price` and `Price` are two different names.
Do not use Python's own words, such as `True`, `None` or `class`.

segments.say: Good names make code easy to read. Python has rules for names, and its style guide, called pep eight, adds one more.
One, from the style guide. Lowercase words, joined with underscores. Tea price, not a short code like t p.
Two, a rule of Python itself. Letters, digits and underscores are fine, but a name can never start with a digit.
Three. Capital letters matter. Price with a small p and Price with a capital P are two different names.
Four. Do not use the words Python keeps for itself, like True, None or class.

scenes.title: Step 2: Check a type
scenes.direction: Show the four values, teach how Python picks a type, ask, then reveal the type() output.

visual.heading: Step 2: Ask Python for the type

segments.say: Step 2. The type function tells you the type of any value. Asha stores four values from her cafe.
Python picks each type from the way you wrote the value. A decimal point makes a float. Quotation marks make a string.
Lines 6 to 9 print each value, followed by its type.

ask.question: Which type will Python report for `price` on line 7?

after.say: Float, because 3.5 has a decimal point.
And True is a bool. It needs a capital T, or Python will not recognise it.

scenes.title: Step 3: Operators
scenes.direction: Teach what the surprising operators mean first, in general terms. Then the biscuits program, the prediction, and the reveal.

visual.heading: Step 3: Operators that surprise beginners
visual.label: Build it
rows: The full answer, with decimals. Always a `float`.
Only the whole part of the answer.
What is left over after sharing.

segments.say: Step 3. An operator is a symbol that calculates. Plus, minus and times work as you expect. Four others need a closer look.
A single slash divides, and gives the full answer, with decimals. The result is always a float.
A double slash is floor division. It keeps only the whole part of the answer.
The percent sign gives the remainder: what is left over after sharing.
And two stars raise a number to a power.
Asha shares 17 biscuits between 5 friends. Add, subtract and multiply are straightforward.
Now use what you learned about the other operators.

ask.question: Predict lines 7, 8 and 9: divide, floor divide and remainder.

after.say: Divide gives 3.4, the full answer, as a float.
Floor divide gives 3. Each friend gets three whole biscuits.
And the remainder is 2. Two biscuits are left over, probably for Asha.

scenes.title: Step 4: Change a variable
scenes.direction: Teach the right-side-first rule on line 4, then let the learner apply it to line 6.

segments.say: Step 4. Asha runs a loyalty game. Points starts at 10.
Line 4 looks impossible in maths: points equals points plus 5. But remember the rule. Python works out the right side first.
So it takes the current value, 10, adds 5, and moves the name to 15.
Now line 6 doubles it, using the same rule.

after.say: After the bonus, 30. Fifteen, times 2.

scenes.title: Step 5: Order of operations
scenes.direction: Teach the order rule, then predict two lines, then the float surprise and round(). Then a quiz and a breather.

visual.heading: Step 5: Which part goes first?
visual.label: Order of operations
items: First: `**`
Last: `+` and `-`
Brackets go before everything.

segments.say: Step 5. When a line has several operators, Python follows the same order as maths.
Powers first.
Then times, and every kind of division.
Plus and minus come last.
And brackets beat everything. Whatever is inside them is calculated first.
Lines 2 and 3 use the same numbers. Only the brackets are different.

after.say: Line 2 multiplies first: 3 times 4 is 12, plus 2 is 14.
Line 3 adds first, because of the brackets. 5 times 4 is 20.
Line 4 divides first, so you get 8.0. A float, because a single slash always gives one.
Now line 5. Point 1, three times, should be point 3. But look! Computers store decimals in binary, so some values carry a tiny error.
The round function gives you a rounded number. Here, to two decimal places.

segments.say: Quick check. Two plus four, in brackets, times three. What does it give?

after.say: B, 18. The brackets go first: 6, times 3.

items: `/` gives a `float`; `//` keeps the whole part; `%` gives the rest.
The right side of `=` runs first.
Brackets control the order.

messages.text: I am a beginner learning Python variables. I want the average bill of three cafe tables: 18, 24 and 30. Do not write code yet. List the variables I need, with a snake_case name and a type for each.

1. `bill_1`, `bill_2` and `bill_3`: type `int`, values 18, 24 and 30.
2. `average`: the sum of the three bills divided by 3. Its type is `float`, because `/` always gives a `float`.

segments.say: Stage 1: plan. Asha describes the average in words, and asks for the variables she needs. No code yet.
The AI lists three bills as ints, and an average as a float. That matches the rule you learned: a single slash always gives a float.

messages.text: I wrote the first lines myself. Do not change them. Do my names follow PEP 8, and what type is each value?

Yes. All three names are lowercase words joined by underscores.
Each value is an `int`, because it is a whole number with no decimal point.

segments.say: Stage 2: write. Asha writes the first three lines herself, one bill per table. She asks the AI to check her names and the types, without changing anything.
The AI agrees. The names follow the style rule, and each bill is an int, a whole number. Asha predicted the same.

messages.text: Now complete my program. Keep my three bill lines, add a line that finds the average of the bills with the name average, and print it. Tell me exactly what it prints.
Here is the program. It prints `Average bill: 24.0`.
I ran it. This is what it printed:

segments.say: Stage 3: generate. Asha asks the AI to complete her program with the average, and to say exactly what it prints.
The AI writes the program, and says it prints 24.0. It sounds sure.
Look at line 5. You learned which part Python calculates first.

ask.question: The AI says this prints `Average bill: 24.0`. Is it right?

after.say: Asha runs it. 52.0! The AI was wrong, and it sounded completely sure.

visual.heading: Test: is the result even possible?

messages.text: You predicted 24.0, but it printed 52.0. An average must lie between the smallest and the largest bill, and the largest is 30. What is wrong?
Python divides before it adds, so only `bill_3` was divided by 3. Put brackets around the sum:

segments.say: Stage 4: test. Here is a quick sense check for any average. It must lie between the smallest and the largest value. The largest bill is 30, so 52 is impossible.
She tells the AI what it predicted and what really happened. Now it names the cause: Python divided before it added. Brackets fix the order.
Asha runs the fixed version. 24.0. Now the prediction and the real run agree.

visual.heading: Debug: the cause before the fix

messages.text: I typed the program again in my own file and got this error. First explain what it means and which line causes it. Then show the smallest fix.

It is a `NameError` on line 6. You created `average`, but line 6 uses `averge`, with a missing letter. Python only knows the names you created.
The fix: change `averge` to `average`.

segments.say: Stage 5: debug. Asha types the program into her own file, and Python stops with a Name Error. She pastes the code and the full error.
She asks for the cause first. The AI points to line 6: averge, with a missing letter. Python only knows the names you created.

messages.text: Review my names. Suggest at most two improvements, each with one reason. Do not change what the program prints.

1. Rename `average` to `average_bill`, so a reader knows what it is the average of.
2. Use `//` instead of `/`. Bills are whole numbers, so the average will be cleaner.
Suggestion 2 would change the output. I tested it with a bill of 31 instead of 30:

segments.say: Stage 6: improve. The program works. Asha asks for at most two improvements to her names.
Suggestion 1 is good. Average bill tells a reader what the average is about. Suggestion 2 says: use a double slash, for a cleaner number.
But a double slash keeps only the whole part. Asha tests it with new bills. The double slash drops the point 3 3 3. The AI was wrong again.
So Asha keeps suggestion 1 only. Here is the result: a clear name, brackets around the sum, and a single slash.
The AI helped at every stage. And at every stage, Asha checked its answer herself. Two mistakes caught!

scenes.title: Common mistakes
scenes.direction: Mistake 1 calls back to the debug stage. Mistake 2 pays off the quiz about quotation marks. Mistakes 3 and 4 are spot-it questions on rules taught earlier.

visual.heading: Mistake 1: a typing error in a name

segments.say: Mistake 1 is the one Asha debugged. A name with a typing error. Line 3 printed fine.
Line 4 spells it with an s, so Python stops with a Name Error. It even suggests the right name.
You also get this error if you use a name before the line that creates it.

visual.heading: Mistake 2: a number stored as text

segments.say: Mistake 2. Remember the quick check? A digit in quotation marks is a string, not a number.
Concatenate means join. Python can only join text to text, so it stops with a Type Error.
The fix: remove the quotation marks.
Sometimes this mistake gives no error at all, which is worse. Multiplying a string by 2 repeats the text. So you get 33, not 6.
Without quotation marks, you get 6. If a result looks strange, check its type.

visual.heading: Mistake 3: your turn to spot it
visual.hidden_text: Find the mistake before the error appears.

segments.say: Now you try. Remember the four naming rules from step 1.

ask.question: What is wrong with the name on line 2?

after.say: It starts with a digit. Python reads the 2 as the start of a number, and gets confused by the letters after it.
after.heading: Mistake 3: a name that starts with a digit

after.say: The fix: start with a letter, like second place.

visual.heading: Mistake 4: spot this one too
visual.hidden_text: Find the mistake before the error appears.

segments.say: One more. Think about the assignment diagram from the idea section.

after.say: The name and the value are on the wrong sides. The name always goes on the left.
after.heading: Mistake 4: name and value swapped

after.say: Ten is a literal: a value written straight into the code. A literal cannot be given a new value.

visual.heading: Read the last line first
visual.label: Common mistakes
rows: A typing error in a name
Spell it as you created it

segments.say: Here are all four, by the last line of the error.
Not defined: a typing error in a name.
Can only concatenate: a number stored as text.
Invalid decimal literal: a name that starts with a digit.
Cannot assign to literal: the name is on the wrong side.

visual.heading: Recap
visual.label: What you learned
items: A value is a piece of data, and every value has a type.
A variable is a name for a value. `=` connects the name on the left to the value on the right.
Python works out the right side first, so `points = points + 5` is valid.
`/` always gives a `float`. `//` keeps the whole part; `%` gives the remainder.
Brackets control the order. `round()` tidies an inexact `float`.
Predict, ask the AI to predict, and let the real run decide.

segments.say: Let's recap.
A value is a piece of data, and every value has a type.
A variable is a name for a value. The name goes on the left.
Python works out the right side first, so a variable can use its own old value.
A single slash gives a float. A double slash keeps the whole part, and the percent sign gives the remainder.
Brackets control the order, and round tidies an inexact float.
And with AI: predict, ask, and let the real run decide.

visual.question: `tea_price = 3.5` and `tea_count = 2`. What type is `tea_price * tea_count`?
visual.explain: One part is a `float`, so the result is a `float`: `7.0`.

segments.say: One last check. Tea price is 3.5, and tea count is 2. What type is the tea price times the tea count?

after.say: B. A float. One part was a float, so the result is 7.0, exactly like Asha's bill.
